## R Markdown

This is an R Markdown document. Markdown is a simple formatting syntax for authoring HTML, PDF, and MS Word documents. For more details on using R Markdown see <http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com>.

When you click the **Knit** button a document will be generated that includes both content as well as the output of any embedded R code chunks within the document. You can embed an R code chunk like this:

```{r cars}
summary(cars)
```

## Including Plots

You can also embed plots, for example:

```{r pressure, echo=FALSE}
plot(pressure)
```

Note that the `echo = FALSE` parameter was added to the code chunk to prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.

Question#5
A failed conversation is usually a problem with one value,not the whole program. If R stopped with an error, a single bad entry in a large dataset could halt a long script. A warning lets the script keep running, and R puts NA in place of the vale it couldn't convert.
The NA values can carry through the rest of your analysis without being noticed. Average and sums can come out as NA or wrong, and rows can be dropped without you realing. The script finishes without an error, so you might trust results that are incomplete or incorrect.
Question#6
```{r}
as.logical(2)
as.logical(-1)
```
Testing confirms both return TRUE. R follows this rule: 0 converts to FALSE, and any non-zero number converts to TRUE, whether it's positive, negative, or a decimal.

Question#7
paste() and paste0() gave different result because they use different default separators. paste() has sep = " " by deafault, so it puts a space between each string it joins. paste0() is the same as paste() so it puts nothing between them. With the same two strings
Question#8
No, it did not  cause an error. Internally,paste0() converts each its arguments to character before joining them. So the number 21 becomes the string "21", and then it is joined with the other text. This is the same kind of coercion from Part C, whwer as.character() turns a number into text. The difference is that in Part C you called the conversion yourself, and here paste0() does it for you automatically

```{r}
as.numeric("5") + 5
```
Question#9
R requires explicit conversion because it's designed to be predictable and safe rather than " helpful by guessing. " If R silently converted types, a programmer might not notice when their data is actually the wrong type
Question#10
The column is likely stored as text (character), not numeric, probably due to stay symbols, commas, spaces, or blanks from the file import. To fix it: check typeof()/class() to confirm the type, inspect the raw values for hidden characters, clean the data, then convert with as.numeric(), watching for NA warinings that flag which values failed.
Conclusion
R enforces strict typing instead of guessing, so data that looks numeric may not actually be. typeof()/class() help confirm the real type, and conversion functions like as.numeric() (with attention to warnings) let you fix mismatches safely before doing math.
